A Note to the Parent
First of all, thank you for picking up this book. You’re doing something
important by taking your teenager’s financial education into your own
hands, and I deeply respect that. I wrote this book with my own three
children in mind, so I know exactly how much you care about setting
your child up for success.
 This book isn’t meant to be an academic textbook. It’s
intentionally written in a voice that teenagers can relate to—because
talking about money can feel abstract, boring, or even stressful at that
age.
 Financial literacy should be practical, straightforward, and human.
 The ideas here are timeless. They’re the same principles that most
people who’ve built and kept wealth have followed—regardless of
background or personality. These are tools that can last a lifetime and
span generations. What this book isn’t: It’s not a deep dive into
investments or complex financial strategies. That can come later, when
the time is right. Right now, your job is to encourage your teen to
understand how money flows in and out of their life, and how their
choices can either make money work for them or against them.
 I believe money skills are like seeds: once planted, they tend to
grow. If a teen starts to understand the basic concepts—things like
earning, saving, risk, and time—they will begin to see money
differently. And often, they’ll run with it.
 Every chapter concludes with a summary and some action steps. I
encourage you to read those together or simply ask about them. Your
experience—successes, mistakes, and perspective—is the most
powerful teaching tool. When you talk about real-life implications, the
lessons become real. They stick.

 To be honest, I didn’t grow up with a silver spoon. I attended
regular schools in Sweden and had a fairly typical childhood—not at

the top of the class, just curious. My big break came when my family
moved to the UK. Suddenly, I felt plugged into the world. Like a
Viking with a backpack, I wanted to explore. I studied in both the UK
and the US and eventually became a trader in the City of London. That
career gave me a front-row seat to how the financial world works—and
it also opened the world itself.
 Over the years, I’ve had the privilege of traveling the world for
work. And what I found, wherever I went, was that people have
remarkably similar dreams: more freedom, more opportunity, a better
future for themselves and their families. And sooner or later, those
dreams almost always bring us back to the topic of money.
 I didn’t come from wealth. I didn’t have connections in the
banking world. When I applied for my first job, I couldn’t even afford
stamps, so I hand-delivered every application. Everything I’ve built has
come from effort—hard work, curiosity, and the decision to become
financially savvy. I’ve spent 25 years learning how to earn it, save it,
and make it work for me. But that doesn’t mean I’ve “made it” or
stopped working. Life keeps changing, and money skills only matter if
you can adapt. What matters most isn’t how much you have—it’s how
well you understand it and what you do with it.
 I’ve written these pages to pass on what I’ve learned—from my
career and from being a parent. If this book helps your teen take even
one step toward more confidence and independence with money, it’s
done its job.
 Thanks again for trusting me with a small part of your family’s

INTRODUCTION
 This Could Change Everything

“The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second-best
time is today.” – Chinese Proverb

Do you want more freedom in your life? More choices? Less stress
about money? Financial literacy is a tool that helps you build a more
rewarding life.
 This isn’t about being good at math or becoming rich overnight.
It’s about knowing how money works—so you can make better
decisions, avoid dumb mistakes, and start building the life you want
on your terms. The good news? You already have everything you need
to put this knowledge into action. All you need to do is plant that seed.
 Imagine your life like a road trip. You don’t know the exact
destination yet. Maybe you’ll launch a business, travel the world, or
become a doctor or artist. But whatever your path, you’ll need fuel to
move forward. Money is that fuel. And financial literacy? That’s your
map. If you don’t know how to read that map, you risk getting lost,
taking wrong turns, running out of gas, or depending on someone else
to drive.
 But if you learn to earn, save, grow, and spend wisely, you’ll be in
the driver’s seat. You’ll make your calls. This isn’t something to wait
on. The earlier you learn it, the more power you have. That’s not

you’ll be in
the driver’s seat. You’ll make your calls. This isn’t something to wait
on. The earlier you learn it, the more power you have. That’s not

motivational fluff, it’s math. Every year you delay, the harder it gets to
catch up.
 You may wonder, “Why should I care about this now?” Because
most people only learn the hard way. They get paid and go broke. They
borrow and drown in debt. They chase success but lose control. And
it’s not because they’re lazy or reckless, but because nobody ever taught
them how money works.
 I’ve had the good fortune to see the world up close. I’ve lived and
worked on five continents. But don’t mistake that for a straight path
or a perfect résumé. I’ve taken some impressively stupid risks with both
my career and my money.
 Early on, I turned down the chance to work directly for someone
who later became co-CEO of Deutsche Bank—because I didn’t see the
point at the time. Around the same period, I blew all my savings on a
complete wreck of a car. I once spent almost everything I had on blue
sapphires from a market in Thailand while backpacking. (Spoiler: I
didn’t, but it was close.)
 The amazing thing with life is that if you pay attention, life teaches
you. If you learn from your mistakes, you get better at steering through
what it throws at you. And just when you think you’ve got it all figured
out, life will school you again. That’s the beauty of it. You never really
arrive.
 Money plays into all of that. It reflects how you’ve spent your time,
energy, and attention. In a way, it becomes a kind of stored life force.
And time? Time becomes increasingly valuable as you age. So learning
how money works now, while you’re still young, is one of the smartest
investments you can make. Learn from other people’s mistakes—
including mine. You’ll still make your own, and that’s okay. The goal
isn’t perfection—it’s progress. Level up, one decision at a time.
 With financial freedom, I’ve begun to live a life that’s more aligned
with my own values. I stepped away from the New York–London–
Singapore career track and chose sunny Portugal instead. I changed
gears. I changed my cost base. And I gained time—time to spend with

 I wrote this book because I’ve seen what happens when people
don’t learn this early in life. I spent 25 years in investment banking,
then became a coach helping people rebuild their lives after losing jobs,
careers, and even their sense of identity. And I’ve seen this truth again
and again: money won’t solve everything, but understanding it can save
you from a lot of pain.
 I also wrote this as a parent. I have three kids. Two are teenagers.
I wanted them, and you, to have something I never had: a clear, real-
world guide to money that makes sense at your age.
 At the end of each chapter, you’ll find simple takeaways and action
steps. You’ll learn even faster if you talk them through with someone
you trust, such as a parent, a coach, or a trusted adult. Ask them about
their experiences with money.
 Don’t worry if you don’t get it all at once. What matters is that
you start. By the end, you’ll see that financial literacy isn’t about being
perfect — it’s about being prepared. And since this journey’s more fun
with company, I’d like you to meet three people who’ll be travelling
alongside you through these pages. They’re just like you — figuring
out life, money, and what it all means.
 You might identify more with one than another, and that’s great.
There’s no “right” personality when it comes to money — just your
own. The key is being aware of who you are: what you’re good at, what
trips you up, and how to fine-tune your spidey senses so you know when
to sit up and pay attention — and when you can relax. The real secret
to success isn’t being perfect. It’s knowing your weak spots so you can
build better habits.

Did you know that young people who learn about money at an early
age are far more likely to succeed later in life? A global review of
dozens of studies found that teens who get financial education
understand money better and make smarter choices with saving,
spending, and avoiding debt as adults. In other words, learning how
to manage money now helps you crush it later.

But before we talk about earning or spending, let’s pause and get real
about one thing:

What are you actually trying to achieve?

For me, success wasn’t about hitting a number or winning a title; it was
about freedom. I wanted to break free from the grind and live on my
terms. So, I saved and invested with one goal in mind: independence.
But you know what? The real success didn’t come the day I left my
corporate job. It came after. It came in the mornings when I could
show up fully for my kids. In the lunches where I could roll on the mat
and train in Jiu-Jitsu. In the slow hours of writing and coaching around
the things that matter most to me. Success isn’t a finish line; it’s how
you feel after you’ve crossed it. If you’re not building a life you enjoy,
then what are you working so hard for?

WHAT DOES SUCCESS MEAN TO YOU?

That’s one version of success — mine. But for someone like Jade,
success looked completely different. It wasn’t about escaping the grind;
it was about enduring it until the right door opened.

So, let’s back up and start with the one thing most people skip: defining
what success means to you. Not your parents, not your friends, not
social media, but you.
 Is it freedom? Creating something meaningful? Having a family?
Buying your first place by 25? Whatever it is, define it early. That way,
the rest of this book and the financial journey you’re about to go on
will get you somewhere you want to be.
 Now that you’ve taken a moment to ask yourself what success
means to you, let’s break it down even further—because success and
failure aren’t always what they seem. You might think that success
means earning a lot of money or getting perfect grades. But real success
often looks a lot messier than that. Sometimes, it’s just about progress.
Sometimes, it’s about getting up after you’ve been knocked down. And
sometimes, success is simply learning from failure and doing better
next time.

Defining Success vs. Failure
Success and failure are personal; they mean different things to
everyone. For example, if you get a lower grade than expected but learn
what to improve, that is a success because you are growing. If you fail
to score a goal in soccer but work harder next time, that is progress.
Failure is not the opposite of success; it’s a step toward it. How you see
failure shapes how you bounce back.

Success
Success is very subjective; it can come in many different forms. Think
about the following:

Achievement of goals: You set goals, plan, and execute. If you deliver
on your goals as expected, you feel a sense of success. You did it. Your
journey to deliver on your goals might be littered with failures as you
discover more than one way of not doing it. You persevered and stood
up to the challenge.

Fulfilment and Satisfaction: Feeling fulfilled or satisfied because you
tried your best. Imagine that you studied hard for a test but did not get
the desired grade. You might still feel fulfilled and satisfied. Perhaps
you also learned how to achieve a better result next time. You can’t ask
for more than that. That is a success.

Positive results and emotions: When an outcome is better than
expected, you might feel that you have succeeded, or at least it was not
a complete failure. Emotions and outcomes are linked through
expectations.

Progress and growth: Personal development and growth are successes
in themselves. Working to improve yourself and overcoming obstacles
and challenges leads to levelling up. It may be hard to observe now, but

Failure
The important thing about failure is that it has a bad reputation. But
failure’s reputation is not accurate. We all have to fail; it is a normal
part of life. How else do we learn?

Failure can look something like:

Not achieving the goals you set out to achieve: You feel awful and
beat yourself up, tuning in to negative emotions. How bad you feel and
how long you remain in the state all depend on your expectations
before the event and the efforts you put into it. How quickly you
bounce back depends on your ability to put things into perspective and
turn this failure into another step to success.

Defining Success in Terms of Money
For some people, success is defined by the amount of money they have.
But money is just a tool; it is not the goal. True success with money
means:

• You are not constantly stressed about not having any.
 • You can save for things that matter.
 • You can handle change.

The Recipe for Lasting Success
Here’s the truth: if you’re not happy with where you are right now,
you first need to acknowledge that. Not everything has to be perfect.
But if you’re ignoring that something feels off—financially,
emotionally, or otherwise—you’re not doing yourself any favors. Take
ownership of that feeling. Don’t sugarcoat it. Then, do something
about it. Success doesn’t have to be flashy. It doesn’t have to mean a
big house, a PhD, or a six-figure salary—unless those are things you
want, and you’ve mapped out why. If you’re going to work for
something, make sure it’s something you care about, not just
something that looks good on paper or makes others nod approvingly.
 Ask yourself: Am I living in a way aligned with who I am and what
I care about? If not, what’s one small step I can take to shift the
direction? You don’t have to overhaul everything overnight. Just start
with clarity and honesty. That’s the beginning of a real financial
strategy—and a fulfilling life.

 Well done! That is an amazing feat. However, you are now in your

 Suppose you invested those $300,000 and practiced a bit of
delayed gratification while enjoying the compound effect at work.
How would that compare to your expected reward? Your new career
might give you incredible daily satisfaction. Still, you may have no
money to maintain the standard of living you expected, as you are now
in debt. You might also not enjoy your career as much, as you never
had the opportunity to practice it professionally, given that you went
straight from university to pursue your PhD. How could you know? If
you are enjoying your new career and feel like you’re being fairly
rewarded, that is great. If not, then you have some hard choices to
make. As you just invested the best part of ten years pursuing higher
education, you might feel forced to accept the result and get on with
it. Respect, maybe; happiness, not so much.
 To achieve real, lasting success, pursue your passion as soon as you
recognize it. It’s okay if it changes. You will pivot, and you are likely

Summary: What Does Success Mean to You?
Success isn’t about what other people think—it’s about what matters
to you. In this chapter, you explored how defining your version of
success is the first step toward using money wisely. Without clarity,
you risk chasing goals that leave you stressed, broke, or unfulfilled. You
also learned that failure is not the opposite of success—it’s part of the
process. Financial wins (and losses) should always tie back to what you
value. Your job is to determine what that is and build your financial
goals around it. When you do, financial literacy becomes a superpower
to help you turn your dreams into real-life outcomes.

Key Takeaways

• Success is personal—define it for yourself before
 chasing goals.
 • Failure is normal; it’s feedback, not defeat.
 • Money is a tool to support your definition of success—
 not the goal itself.
 • Your long-term happiness depends on aligning goals
 with values.
 • Real success includes financial stability, not just flashy
 achievements.

What even is money? It’s not just coins or numbers on a screen. Money
is a tool. And like any tool, it’s only useful if you know what to do with
it. It’s not the goal; it’s what helps you reach your goals. No matter if
your vision of success is travel, freedom, fun, or independence, money
is part of the fuel that gets you there.
 So the real question isn’t “How much money do I want?” It’s:
“What do I want my life to look like—and how will money help me
build that?”
 Poor financial knowledge makes decision-making harder, increases
your risk of falling into debt traps, and leaves you struggling to
understand why saving even matters.
 But here’s the thing: learning about money early can change your
life in amazing ways. You’ll understand how to:

• Avoid credit card traps and high-interest debt.

a little bit every time you receive money. Even if it’s small, regular
savings build momentum. They give you options, and they let you plan
your life instead of reacting to every emergency. We will discuss saving

Summary: Delayed Gratification
Delayed gratification is one of the most important skills you can
develop, especially when it comes to managing your finances. It’s the
habit of choosing long-term gain over quick rewards, and it separates
people who stay stuck from those who grow into the lives they want.
 In a world that delivers everything instantly—food, fashion,
entertainment—it’s easy to get trapped in the cycle of “I want it now.”
But that shortcut comes with a cost. When you constantly borrow from
your future for short-term pleasure, you lose freedom, build debt, and
stay stuck chasing the next hit. This chapter explored how saving, staying
focused, and consistently showing up can create big, long-term results.
Whether training for a sport, building a business, or learning a skill, the
same rule applies: small actions add up. That’s the compound effect—
and it’s a superpower. We also discussed how passion alone isn’t always
enough. You might love something deeply, but without a plan, it won’t
always pay the bills. Flexibility, strategy, and delayed gratification help
you turn dreams into reality without burning out or giving up.

Summary: Time, Your Greatest Asset
Time is the one resource you can’t earn more of. Once it’s spent, it’s
gone. And yet, many people waste it without realizing they’re giving
away their most powerful asset. This chapter unpacks why time is the
secret supercharger of your financial journey. Unlike money, which can
be lost and regained, time only moves in one direction. That’s why
learning to manage it well is one of the smartest money skills you can
develop.
 Used wisely, time fuels the compound effect—the principle that
small, consistent actions accumulate into significant rewards. Whether
it’s saving, investing, learning a skill, or building habits, time makes
those actions meaningful. But if you waste your hours on distractions,
procrastination, or impulse decisions, you’re burning energy that could
have built a better future.
 Understanding the value of time also means seeing its connection to
money. Concepts like inflation, interest, and opportunity cost
demonstrate how your time choices impact the value of your money,
and how much freedom it can buy. Time turns effort into momentum,
rest into recovery, and values into action. And because everyone gets the
same 24 hours a day, how you use yours determines how far you go.

they are already here, already changing what work looks like, already
making traditional career paths less predictable. With the rise of social
media, teens now face constant comparison and pressure to have all the
answers about their future.
 What many young people don't have yet is a way of thinking about

shape decades of their lives.

them to slow down and think clearly instead.

You will spend roughly 90,000 hours of your life working. That is an
uncomfortable amount of time to spend doing something you hate.
Do the maths — eight hours a day, five days a week, from around
twenty-one until you retire at sixty-six. That's more time than you'll
spend with your family, your friends, or even sleeping.

their jobs. Which means millions of people are basically renting out
their best energy to something they don't love. They’re disengaged,
going through the motions, living for the weekend.
 Careers aren’t just about jobs. They shape your lifestyle, your
freedom, your stress, and your happiness. And yet, almost no one talks
to you about that when you’re young. We tell you to pick subjects,
pick a college, pick a path—but we rarely ask the better question: What
kind of life do you want your career to give you?

My Train Moment
London Underground. 2018. I was wedged into a carriage at rush
hour. Nothing unusual about the day. I was a few years shy of fifty,
with a great title and a great pay cheque. On paper, my career looked
amazing.
 Inside, I felt hollow. I had won the race I thought I was supposed
to win and somehow still felt like I had lost.
 Most days, I was in an office, on a plane, or glued to my phone. I
wasn’t really present anywhere. My days no longer felt like they
belonged to me. I barely saw my kids. As the train lurched forward and
I grabbed the rail, the thought hit me like a wave: I’m just another link
in a chain gang, moving but not going anywhere that matters to me.
 Sure, I had money. But I didn’t have freedom. I didn’t have
balance. And I had to ask myself: Is this what I want? Is this what I’m
trading my time and family for?
 I’d told myself the classic story: go to work, make money, and one
day you’ll finally do what you love. But life doesn’t work like that. At
twenty, starting over feels easy. At fifty, when people depend on you,
it isn’t.
 How did I get here? Honestly, I followed my older brother’s
footprints. It was the obvious path. One “yes” after another—
promotion, project, pay rise—and suddenly, there I was. That is how
drifting works — not with one terrible decision, but with a thousand
unexamined sensible ones.

Ask five friends what success means, and you’ll get five different
answers: making money, being famous, having freedom to travel,
building something that matters, and feeling happy most days. All

 My own path went from banking to writing and coaching — and
I'm not done yet. Things change. You adapt. No single definition
covers every season of a life.
 FOMO gets loudest when you have not chosen your own lane.
The antidote is knowing your values and checking in with them often.
 Social media is a highlight reel. No one posts their worst day. You
don’t see the failed test, the ugly cry after an argument, the morning
you couldn’t get out of bed. You see trophies, perfect coffees,
promotions, vacations—a constant stream of wins. When your feed is

 Real life—and real careers—don’t work like that. Real success is

practising when no one’s watching, finishing a hard assignment. People
who celebrate those tiny steps are often closer to genuine success than

process.

Jade once asked a teacher, “So… a career is the job you pick when
you’re eighteen, and then you just keep doing it?”
 The teacher laughed kindly and said, “If that were true, my life

what they did—Smith, Miller, Cooper, Butcher. Work was often
generational: kids became apprentices to their parents and carried on
the family trade. But that’s now the exception, not the rule. Our
grandparents often worked at one company for decades. It was stable,
predictable, like playing a game with long levels—you just kept
showing up and eventually “levelled up.” Today, careers behave
nothing like that. Technology moves so fast that whole industries rise
and vanish before your phone contract even renews. Think about apps
everyone swore would last forever—Vine, BBM, BeReal—gone or
forgotten. The trends you thought were permanent age faster than
memes. Careers now live in that same kind of world: shifting, glitching,
updating constantly.
 It’s like playing a video game where every new level is shorter than
the last. To stay in the game, you need to level up quicker—learn new
skills, adapt to new tools, and sometimes switch strategies completely.

Routes, Rest Stops, and Dead Ends
Your planned route is the theme you choose for reaching your goal.
Rest stops mark the end of a journey leg. Maybe you need to study at
university to acquire certain skills, and when that is done, it marks the
end of a leg on your journey, a rest stop. You refill, get some snacks
and go again.
 A route change is when you decide you are not enjoying the
current one. Things may be going too slowly, there may be too much
traffic, or there may be too little traffic. Think about it as taking your
skills and applying them in a new direction. For example, a biology
student who changes from pre-med to medical research. Or a varsity
athlete who pivots from accounting to sports performance analytics.
The destination is still the same field, but the route better matches your
skills and energy.

the destination itself has changed. You might need to make a U-turn

My Own Career Journey
I didn’t exactly plan to work in finance—it kind of happened. One
step led to another, and before I knew it, I had spent twenty-five years
in investment banking. The thing about that world is there’s no “cruise
control.” You either perform, or you’re out. It was exciting, sure, but
also cutthroat. Money can make people go a little crazy.
 For most of my career, the job description didn’t change: watch
the markets, take risks, make money. But the environment? That
changed massively. I started with phones and notepads; by the end, I
was competing with algorithms. The human part of the job slowly
disappeared—and so did my joy.
 After twenty-five years, the industry and I kind of broke up. It
wasn’t dramatic, more like: “Thanks for the ride, but we’re done.”
Suddenly, I was left with a question: What now?

probably could have kept fighting, training harder, chasing that tiny
window of possibility. The real question was: did I want to? Was I
willing to put in that level of grind for the life that came with it?
 Because here’s the part nobody tells you when they say, “Never give
up on your dreams.” We all have a lot of dreams—and some are better,
more realistic, and more worth chasing than others. The trick isn’t
refusing to give up; it’s learning which dreams deserve your time,
energy, and future. It’s not quitting—it’s choosing wisely.
 I got a try-out at Rutgers in New Jersey. Within days, it was clear—
to the coaches and me—that I’d struggle to make the travelling team.
The talent around me was real. I was fighting to be one of eight players
on a team that, with no disrespect to Rutgers tennis in the 90s, wasn’t
exactly a national powerhouse. Then my brain did something annoying
and useful at the same time: it zoomed out. I pictured all the other
teams across the U.S., then the world—thousands of players with more
power, more years of grind, more everything.
 Here’s the part I hadn’t really looked at: the money. The
scholarship only covered you if you made the team. If you didn’t, you

 Meanwhile, I did the other math: if I pivoted to coaching, the

 So I made the call. I could keep grinding, maybe make the team,
maybe not. But even if I did, the path ahead didn’t match the life I

When you invest money, interest builds on interest. That’s called
compound growth.
 We talked about this in Money Starts With You—it’s what happens
when you make a habit of saving or investing and let time and patience
do their thing. The longer you stay consistent, the more your results
grow. Magic, right? Well, learning works in the same way.

about angles and geometry. Then you take a physics class and start
understanding how certain materials bend and hold weight. Put those
together and suddenly you’ve got the foundations for building a really
strong house. That’s compound learning. Each new piece of knowledge
adds strength to the last.

There’s one big misconception floating around today: if it’s really hard

 Just because a job is hard to get doesn’t mean it’s good—at least,
not good for you. The starting pay might be incredible, and sure, that
looks great on paper (and on Instagram). But sometimes that big pay
cheque is actually the biggest trap. It comes with conditions—long
hours, relentless expectations, pressure that eats into your sleep, your
health, your relationships. It can set a tempo that drags you along for
years, doing something that looks impressive but doesn’t feel right.

crowds,” I call it—all marching toward the same shiny set of careers

doesn’t have to look like anyone else’s.

Here’s a quiet metric that matters: if you can free up time, you’re

your earning potential later. That’s delayed gratification—trading a bit

somewhere that feeds your soul.

me time to level up and learn? Will my stress stay low enough for me

long-term, or am I trading energy I won’t get back?

INTRODUCTION
 Why I Wrote This Book & How to Use It
Growing up in the 80s was blissful ignorance. We didn’t have the
internet, social media, or a constant stream of other people’s highlight
reels. Life felt simpler—but in a strange way, that simplicity left me
completely unprepared for what was waiting once I stepped into the
real world.
 I had no idea how tough the transition from school to adulthood
would be. The expectations, the setbacks, the feeling that I was
supposed to have it all figured out—it hit me hard. That transition hit
hard. Disappointment can be overwhelming, and when you start to feel
like a failure, it’s like carrying a lead weight around your neck.
 That’s the thing about growing up—no one warns you that success
doesn’t just depend on grades, goals, or effort. It depends on how well
you understand yourself when life doesn’t go to plan. And that’s where
self-leadership begins.
 Growing up, my inspiration wasn't a pop star or a footballer. It was
Björn Borg — a tennis player who dominated the world in the late 70s
and early 80s with a focus and drive that felt almost inhuman. What
struck me wasn't the trophies. It was the simplicity. He got to the top
of the world by doing one thing really well, with complete dedication.
No noise. No shortcuts. Just relentless commitment to his craft.
 But here's what nobody talked about back then — the mental cost.
The pressure. The fact that he walked away from the sport at 26, at the

“Success.”
 It’s a word you probably hear everywhere—at school, online, from
parents, teachers, and people who seem like they’ve got life figured out.
 But here’s the strange thing: no one seems to agree on what success
actually means.
 Some people say it’s grades, trophies, money, or followers. Others
say it’s popularity, confidence, or being seen as “winning.”
 And if you asked ten people to define success, you’d probably get
ten different answers.
 That’s why it’s important to figure out your own meaning early on.
Because how you define success will shape how you act, what you aim
for, and how you measure your progress.
 So… what does success mean to you? Is it something you can see—
like grades, clothes, or awards? Or something you can feel—like
happiness, peace, or confidence?
 I can’t tell you what success should mean for you—it’s personal.
But I can tell you this: real success isn’t built on stuff alone.
 Take grades, for example. If you get straight As but still don’t feel
happy or proud of yourself, is that success? What about when you buy
something new—shoes, a phone, whatever— and it feels amazing for a
few days… until it doesn’t? That’s because success built only on things
or validation from others doesn’t last.

in the parts of life that feel messy or hard.

then, out of nowhere, something connects—a move I’ve been failing at

lines up, is proof that all those “stuck” days were part of the process.
 That’s how growth works. You study something for months, think
you’ll never need it, and then one day you do—and suddenly, you get
it.

today than you were yesterday. You don’t need to compare your speed
or distance to anyone else’s. You can’t drive their vehicle—only yours.

away from you. What you learn, the strength you build, the experiences

survive, but you like it—it tastes better, it makes you feel good. So even

Self-leadership isn’t something you can buy or that magically appears
after reading the right book or listening to the right person. It isn’t an
idea you memorise, and it isn’t a theory you store somewhere in the
back of your mind, hoping it will activate when needed. Self-leadership
is something you do. It shows up in your choices, your behaviour, the
small moments when no one is watching, and the quiet decisions you
make about who you want to be.

Self-leadership lives in action.

It is the set of conscious actions you take with the intention—not the
pressure, just the intention—to become a slightly better version of
yourself than you were yesterday. Sometimes that effort feels steady and
natural, like you’re simply following the path your life is already opening
for you. Other times, it feels like you’re pushing uphill in the dark, trying
to find your footing when everything seems uncertain. But either way,
self-leadership is the force that moves you forward, the part of you that
keeps choosing growth even when it would be easier to stay still.
 And here’s something people don’t talk about enough: self-
leadership feels different depending on where you are in your personal
journey. When you’ve already discovered something that matters
deeply to you—a dream, a talent, a curiosity, a direction that feels
meaningful—self-leadership starts to act like a pull. You don’t need to
force yourself as much; there is a natural desire that draws you forward.
It’s the wind in your sails. Your role becomes one of looking after your
energy, organising your time, and making sure you’re in the best possible
shape, inside and out, to move toward what you care about. In that phase,
self-leadership feels like alignment: you want it, and you’re willing to
work for it.
 But if you’re not there yet—if your purpose still feels murky,
distant, or completely unknown—then self-leadership takes a different
form. It becomes more of a push, not because you’re forcing yourself into
a direction you dislike, but because you’re opening doors, exploring
possibilities, and creating the exposure that will eventually help you
discover what feels right. Purpose isn’t something you stumble upon like
a hidden treasure; it’s something you build through curiosity,
experimentation, habits, and the willingness to learn who you are
through action. And self-leadership is the guide that keeps you moving,
even when you don’t yet know where the path will lead.
 A lot of teenagers believe that purpose is something you
“discover”—a lightningbolt moment, a sudden clarity, a perfect identity
that snaps into place. But the truth is quieter and much more reassuring:
purpose is built. It grows out of choices, patterns, experiences, and the
courage to try things even when you’re unsure. You shape it slowly by

Here’s the deal: the way you move through the world matters far more
than you realise. I’ve always had a little saying—be good and do good—

When you choose to do good things, even small ones, the universe has

the one you imagined, but it does respond. Sometimes the return arrives
quietly, sometimes it comes from a direction you never saw coming, but
it is always positive, something that nudges your life forward in a way

 When you show up calm, centred, purposeful, and honest about
who you are becoming, you naturally influence the energy around you.
There’s an old saying: smile and the world will smile back at you. It
sounds cheesy, but it’s painfully true. Try this sometime—stare at a
friend with a big, ridiculous grin on your face and watch how long they
last before they crack and smile back. They won’t be able to help
themselves. They’ll probably say, “What? What are you smiling about?”
and suddenly the whole atmosphere shifts.
 People reflect the energy you bring into a room. Friends, family,
classmates, teams, and even total strangers will respond to the version
of you that you choose to present. When you show up consistently with
kindness, steadiness, curiosity, or genuine positivity, it might not
bounce back immediately, but it will. You create a current. A pattern.
A cycle of good energy that eventually returns to you. Not because the
world is perfect or fair— it isn’t—but because humans are built to
respond to the energy around them.
 There will be days when it feels like none of this is working, when

don’t know how to say it out loud, they notice. They see you trying.

moving through life with good intentions rather than bitterness or
avoidance. They see your growth long before you do.

that shifts and changes depending on who is looking at it, and even
then, it is never truly reachable. If perfection ever existed, it would live
entirely in the eye of the beholder, shaped by their standards,
expectations, and mood that day. Perfection is an outcome, something

you’re in—things you can influence, yes, but never command.

process. It is alive, evolving, responsive. Progress is you.

defines you. Every outcome is simply information—feedback you can

your understanding. Outcomes aren’t verdicts. They’re data points.
They show you where you are on your journey, not where you must
end up. Perfection is not the final station, and it cannot be, because

noticing the moment when you’re not.

respond instead of react. Look at the situation and ask: What’s going on?
What do I have? What do I need?

something is missing—support, rest, knowledge, confidence, clarity.

having everything; it’s about moving toward what you need, one step
at a time.

failing at life. You are becoming.

The Time Value of Money, or TVM, is a concept. A dollar today is worth

**1. The Time Value of Money**\
There is a concept in finance that sounds technical but is actually just
common sense once you see it. If I offered you one dollar today or one
dollar a year from now, you would take the dollar today. Every time. Not
because you are impatient, but because you are rational. A dollar today
can be saved, invested, and turned into more than a dollar by the time
that year is up. The future dollar, by comparison, has done nothing. It
has just waited. This is the Time Value of Money. Money today is worth
more than the same amount in the future. And flipped around, future
money is worth less than it appears, because it has not yet had the
chance to grow.

In technical terms, bringing a future amount back to its present value
is called discounting. Here is the formula that captures it:

FV = PV × (1 + r)\^n

FV is the future value, what your money grows into. PV is the present
value, what you start with. r is the rate of return. n is the number of
years.

FV is the future value, what your money grows into. PV is the present
value, what you start with. r is the rate of return. n is the number of
years.

Put simple numbers in and watch what happens. €1,000 invested today at
7% annual return, left alone for ten years, becomes €1,967. The same
€1,000 sitting in a drawer is worth less and less over time as inflation
takes its toll.

Time is either working for you or against you. There is no neutral. The
rate matters. The amount matters. But the variable most people
underestimate, and most consistently waste, is *n*. The number of years.
Because the longer that number gets, the more violent the growth
becomes. Not linear, but exponential. This is why the most important
investment decision you can make right now is not which asset to pick.
It is simply to start.

In finance, we call this Net Present Value, or NPV. The formula looks
like this:

NPV = Σ \[Ct ÷ (1 + r)\^t\] − C0

C0 is what you pay upfront. Ct is the net cash flow you receive in each

You take every future benefit, shrink each one back to what it is worth
in today's money, add them up, and subtract what you paid. If the result
is positive, the numbers support the investment. If it is negative, the
numbers suggest you are overpaying for the future you are buying. One
thing worth being honest with yourself about is that every number in
that formula is an estimate. The discount rate, the future cash flows,
none of it is guaranteed. The less confident you actually are in those

guess built on assumptions, and how much you trust those assumptions

temperature, and humidity are separate phenomena, but they are all

## Summary

Markets are not random. They are not a casino. They are a system, driven
by real forces that move in predictable directions even when the timing
is uncertain. The central bank controls the price of money through
interest rates, and that single lever moves every asset class
simultaneously. When rates fall, borrowing becomes cheap, future cash
flows are worth more today, and asset prices rise. When rates rise, the
opposite happens. Add the human forces, greed, fear, the patterns that
repeat, and you have a model of how markets actually behave.

## Key Takeaways

-   Markets are driven by real forces, primarily the price of money set
    by central banks, not by random noise.

-   Every asset class responds to interest rate changes, but in
    different ways and by different amounts.

-   The NPV formula connects central bank rates to the value of every
    investment: change the discount rate, and you change the value of
    everything.

-   Greed and fear cause markets to overshoot in both directions. The

cash, not necessarily because it made bad loans, but because the bet
that not everyone would show up at once turned out to be wrong. This is
a bank run. Central banks exist as lenders of last resort to prevent a
confidence crisis becoming a solvency crisis.

**Loose and Tight. The Monetary Policy Cycle**\
The central bank has two modes. Loose, low rates, money flows easily,
activity is stimulated. Tight, high rates, money is expensive, activity
slows, inflationary pressure falls. Every\
investor needs to know where in that cycle they are.

When rates are low, the NPV denominator shrinks. Future cash flows are
worth more today. More projects become profitable. The economy heats up.
When rates are high, the denominator grows. Future cash flows are worth
less. Only high-return projects justify the cost of capital. The economy
cools.

The clue for investors is that if your investment is just breaking even
at the current rate, it is not worth anything on a risk-adjusted basis.
The value of any investment lies in the spread between its return and
the risk-free rate. The wider that spread relative to the risk you are
taking, the more genuine value you capture.

**Quantitative Easing. When Rates Alone are Not Enough**\
Sometimes cutting rates is not enough. In 2008 and again during COVID,
central banks cut to zero or below, and the economy still needed more
support. So they turned to quantitative easing.

QE is simple in concept. The central bank creates new money
electronically and uses it to\
buy government bonds from financial institutions. The sellers receive
cash. Bond prices rise, yields fall further. The cost of borrowing falls
across the whole economy. What few fully anticipated was the scale of
the effect on asset prices. When money costs nothing for years,
investors pile into equities, property, and anything offering a real
return. Prices inflate. People who already own assets get richer. People
who do not, typically younger, just starting out, find it harder to get
on the ladder. The mechanism is not in dispute, even if the politics
around it are.

One important caveat when reading the yield curve during heavy QE: the
curve is no longer a pure market signal. It is being managed. The shape
reflects central bank intentions as much as market expectations. Know
when intervention is happening, because the curve is telling a more
complicated story than it appears.

## The Yield Curve, The Market's Forecast In One Line

Governments borrow across a range of maturities, two years, five, ten,
thirty. Each maturity has a yield attached to it. Plot those yields on a
chart, and you get the yield curve. Normally it slopes upward. Lending
for longer carries more uncertainty, more inflation risk, more
opportunity cost. Investors demand a higher rate for the longer
commitment. A two-year bond yields less than a ten-year bond. That is
the normal shape.\
The curve tells you two things simultaneously: what the market thinks
about the future of\
the economy, and what it thinks about inflation. A steep curve signals
growth expected. A\
flat curve signals uncertainty. An inverted curve, where short rates
exceed long rates, is one of the most closely watched signals in all of
finance.

Inversion happens when the central bank has raised short-term rates
aggressively to fight inflation, but the market believes the economy
will slow and rates will eventually come back down. Long-term investors
buy long bonds to lock in today's rates before they fall, pushing long
yields below short yields. Historically, an inverted US yield curve has
preceded most recessions over the last fifty years. Not immediately,
sometimes with a lag of twelve to eighteen months, but reliably enough
that it is never ignored.

**Government Bonds --- The Benchmark Everything Is Priced Off**\
Every borrower, every company, municipality, foreign government, prices
its debt relative to the benchmark government rate because government
debt is generally treated as the lowest-risk reference point in that
market. It can tax its citizens. It can, in extremis, print money. No
corporate borrower can do either. Credit ratings formalise this. The
highest-rated bonds, US Treasuries, German Bunds, UK Gilts, trade at the
lowest yields. Lower-rated borrowers pay a spread above that benchmark.
A BBB-rated corporate might borrow at government plus 150 basis points.
High yield might be government plus 400. The spread is the market's
price for additional risk.

This is the mental model every investor should carry. Whenever you
consider any investment, you are asking: is the spread between this
return and the risk-free rate large enough to compensate me for the
risk? If the return barely exceeds what you could earn lending to a
government, the investment is probably not worth it.

Beyond rates, central banks can intervene directly in currency markets,
buying their own\

makes exports cheaper. A strong currency makes imports cheaper and helps
control inflation but hurts exporters. A currency weakening too far
imports inflation; everything bought abroad becomes more expensive in
domestic terms. Central banks watch this balance carefully, sometimes
forced to buy their own currency even when looser conditions would
otherwise be called for.

After its property and equity collapse in the early 1990s, the Bank of

## Summary

The central bank is the single most important actor in every investment
market in the world. Not because it controls outcomes, it cannot force
anyone to spend, invest, or lend. But because it controls the price of
money, and the price of money changes the NPV of everything
simultaneously. The yield curve is the market's honest forecast of what
comes next, shaped by millions of investors making millions of decisions
in real time. Learn to read it, and you will be far better prepared for
a recession, a rate change, or a market correction that others call
unexpected.

-   Low rates shrink the NPV denominator --- future cash flows are worth

-   The yield curve is the market's forecast. An inverted US yield

Calculate: You own a bond paying a 3% coupon, bought when rates were 3%.

money changed. If you hold to maturity, you still get your €10,000 back.

longer the bond, the more sensitive it is to rate moves.

# Appendix 1 --- Key Terms Glossary

Simple definitions of every key term in the book. No jargon. One
sentence each.

**Asset Class:** A category of investment with similar characteristics
and behaviour, the main ones being stocks, bonds, property, cash, and
commodities.

**Bear Market:** A market in sustained decline, typically defined as a
fall of 20% or more from recent highs; usually accompanied by widespread
pessimism.

**Bull Market:** A market in sustained growth, typically defined as a
rise of 20% or more --- usually accompanied by investor confidence and
rising prices.

**Compounding:** The process by which returns generate their own returns
over time, the mathematical engine that turns consistent small
investments into significant wealth.

**Discount Rate:** The interest rate used to calculate the present value
of future cash flows, the higher the rate, the less future money is
worth today.

**Diversification:** Spreading investments across different asset
classes, sectors, and geographies so that no single loss can devastate
the whole portfolio.

sification:** Spreading investments across different asset
classes, sectors, and geographies so that no single loss can devastate

**Dividend:** A share of a company's profits paid directly to
shareholders, typically quarterly, one of the two ways a stock can
return money to its owner.

**Dollar-Cost Averaging:** Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
regardless of price, so you automatically buy more when prices are low
and less when they are high.

**Duration:** A measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to changes in
interest rates, the longer the bond, the more its price moves when rates
change.

**ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund):** A fund that tracks an index, sector, or
asset class and trades on a stock exchange like a share, combining the
diversification of a fund with the flexibility of a stock.

**Fiat Money:** Currency that has value because a government declares it
legal tender, not because it is backed by a physical commodity like
gold.

**Forward P/E:** A price-to-earnings ratio calculated using projected
future earnings rather than past ones, a measure of what the market
expects, not what has already happened.

expects, not what has already happened.

**Freedom Fund:** Your long-term investment portfolio, funded
consistently, left alone, dividends reinvested, the compounding engine
that builds optionality over time.

**Index Fund:** A fund that tracks a market index such as the S&P 500,
buying every stock in it at market weight; giving broad exposure at very
low cost.

**Inflation:** The rate at which the general price level rises over
time, eroding the purchasing power of money that is not invested or
growing at least as fast.

**Liquidity:** How quickly and easily an asset can be converted into
cash without significantly affecting its price; cash is perfectly
liquid; property is not.

**Market Capitalisation:** The total market value of a company's
outstanding shares, calculated by multiplying the share price by the
number of shares in existence.

**Net Present Value (NPV):** The current value of all future cash flows
from an investment, discounted to reflect the time value of money, a
positive NPV means the investment adds value.

from an investment, discounted to reflect the time value of money, a

**Opportunity Cost:** The value of the best alternative you give up when
making a choice, the true cost of any decision includes not just what
you spend, but what you forgo.

**P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings):** A stock's share price divided by its
earnings per share --- a measure of how much the market is willing to
pay for each euro of profit the company makes.

**Real Return:** The return on an investment after adjusting for
inflation; what your money actually gains in purchasing power, not just
in nominal terms.

**Risk Tolerance:** Your ability and willingness to accept investment
losses in exchange for the possibility of higher returns, shaped by both
your financial situation and your psychology.

**Rule of 72:** A quick formula to estimate how long it takes to double
your money: divide 72 by your annual return. At 7%, your money doubles
approximately every ten years.

**The 25x Rule:** Multiply your desired annual retirement income by 25
to estimate the investment pot you need to build, based on a 4% annual
withdrawal rate.

**Time Value of Money:** The principle that money available today is
worth more than the same amount in the future, because it can be
invested and grown in the meantime.

**Volatility:** The degree to which an asset's price fluctuates over
time, often mistaken for risk, but not the same thing: a volatile asset
may fully recover; a permanent loss does not.

**Yield Curve:** A graph showing interest rates on bonds of the same
credit quality but different maturities, its shape signals what the
market expects from growth and inflation ahead.

Treasury yield; one of the most widely watched recession signals, with
an inverted spread historically preceding many US recessions.
